title: Pareus: the outward act is not the substance of the work
source_text: XLVII. Istud videre est apud Davidem Paraeum saepius jam citatum. Fallit igitur, inquit, & fallitur Bellarminus, externum actum operis, & substantiam operis pro eodem sumendo, quae ut pars & totum differunt. Ad substantiam operis requiritur materia & forma, non minus quam ad substantiam hominis requiritur corpus & anima. Actus externus lege praeceptus est pro materia: interna conformitas & mundities, quae habetur ex fide, est pro forma operis, ad quam finis etiam legitimus requiritur. Nam ipse Philosophus non laudat actum virtutis, nisi ex fine, si fiat τοῦ καλοῦ ἕνεκα. Non igitur qui externum operis actum praestat, substantiam operis praestitit. In Bellarm. lib. V. de Gratia & lib. Arbitrio capite 5.
pass_a_gloss: XLVII. That may be seen in David Pareus already often cited. Bellarmine therefore deceives, he says, and is deceived, by taking the external act of the work, and the substance of the work for the same, which differ as part and whole. For the substance of the work matter and form is required, no less than for the substance of man body and soul is required. The external act commanded by the law is for the matter: the internal conformity and cleanness, which is had from faith, is for the form of the work, to which a lawful end also is required. For the Philosopher himself does not praise an act of virtue, except from the end, if it be done for the sake of the noble. Therefore he who performs the external act of the work, has not performed the substance of the work. On Bellarmine book V on Grace and free Choice chapter 5.
pass_b_english: Thesis XLVII. This can be seen in David Pareus, already cited so often. 'So Bellarmine deceives and is deceived,' he says, 'when he takes the outward act of a work and the substance of the work to be the same thing, though they differ as part and whole. The substance of a work requires matter and form, no less than the substance of a man requires body and soul.

The outward act the law commands serves as the matter. The inward conformity and purity that comes from faith serves as the form of the work, and a lawful end is also required for it. The Philosopher himself praises an act of virtue only on account of its end, if it is done for the sake of the noble. So whoever performs the outward act of a work has not performed the substance of the work' (on Bellarmine, On grace and free choice, book 5, chapter 5).

choices.why: For Pareus the whole work, matter and form together; he denies that the outward act alone, which the Roman School calls the substance, is the substance.
